steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Quantitative data: numerical, can be statistically analysed. Strengths: objective, easy to compare, identifies patterns. Limitations: lacks depth, doesn't explain WHY. Qualitative data: words, rich, detailed. Strengths: captures meaning. Limitations: subjective, hard to generalise.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Primary data: collected by the researcher. Strengths: designed for the question, up-to-date. Limitations: time-consuming. Secondary data: collected by others. Strengths: free, large-scale. Limitations: may lack what's needed.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Correlation does NOT prove causation: two variables change together but a third variable may explain both. Example: poverty and crime rates correlate but deprivation may cause both.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evaluating evidence: consider source (bias?), sample (representative?), method (valid?), date (current?), consistency (confirmed by others?).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between quantitative and qualitative data, evaluating when each is most useful. | Explain why correlation does not prove causation. | A newspaper reports 'crime is rising' based on police statistics. Evaluate this evidence.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Quantitative: numbers, patterns, comparison (best for trends). Qualitative: words, meaning, depth (best for experiences). steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Quantitative = NUMBERS (patterns). Qualitative = WORDS (meaning). TRIANGULATION = both. Correlation is NOT causation. Always consider third variables. Evaluate evidence: SOURCE, SAMPLE, METHOD, DATE, CONSISTENCY.
